title: Percentage
shortDescription: Fractions wearing a percentage costume — strip the costume with the fraction table, and successive changes never simply cancel.
genZNote: Percentages are fractions wearing a tiny % costume. Strip the costume and the math gets easier — 33⅓% of something is just that thing divided by 3.

sections.heading: Core Idea
sections.body: Percentage = (Part/Whole) × 100. The fastest exam approach almost always converts the percentage back to its fraction form first (using the toolkit table) rather than multiplying by a decimal — 25% of 480 as ¼ × 480 = 120 beats 0.25 × 480 for mental speed.

sections.heading: x% of y = y% of x
sections.body: This identity turns an awkward percentage into an easy one by swapping which number plays which role. Example: 8% of 25 is awkward to picture directly, but 25% of 8 = 2 is instant — and both equal the same value.
bullets: Use this whenever ONE of the two numbers is a 'nice' percentage (10, 20, 25, 50) even if the other isn't.

sections.heading: Successive Percentage Change — Does NOT Cancel
sections.body: Percentage change is always relative to the value at THAT step, not the original value — so a rise followed by an equal-magnitude fall does not return to the starting value. Apply each change to the running (already-changed) value, one after another.

steps.name: Worked example — standard method
steps.explanation: A price of ₹200 rises 10%, then the new price falls 10%. After rise: 200 × 1.10 = 220. After fall: 220 × 0.90 = 198.
steps.purpose: Step-by-step application to the running value.

steps.name: Fast method — net % shortcut
steps.explanation: For two successive percentage changes a% and b% (with sign), net % change ≈ a + b + (a×b)/100. Here: 10 + (−10) + (10×−10)/100 = 0 − 1 = −1%.
steps.purpose: Gives the net −1% directly without computing the intermediate value — matches ₹198 from ₹200 (a 1% drop) in one line.

sections.heading: Reverse Percentage
sections.body: When a value AFTER a percentage change is given and you need the ORIGINAL value, divide by (1 ± percentage) rather than trying to reverse-multiply. If a price increased 20% to become ₹360, the original = 360 / 1.20 = ₹300 — not 360 × 0.80, which is a common wrong shortcut.

sections.heading: Percentage Points vs. Percentage Change
sections.body: If a rate moves from 20% to 25%, that is a rise of 5 PERCENTAGE POINTS, but a 25% relative INCREASE in the rate itself ((25−20)/20 × 100 = 25%). Exam questions deliberately mix these two phrasings — read carefully which one is actually being asked for.

sections.heading: Common Traps
bullets: Assuming a rise then an equal fall (or vice versa) cancels out — it never does for non-zero percentages; the net effect is always a decrease.
Computing percentage change by dividing by the NEW value instead of the OLD (original) value.
Reversing a percentage increase by subtracting the percentage instead of dividing by (1 + percentage) to recover the original value.
Confusing 'percentage points' difference with 'percentage change' — they answer different questions.

sections.heading: Exam Strategy
bullets: Convert percentages to fractions from the toolkit table wherever the percentage is a 'nice' one — it's almost always faster than decimal multiplication.
For successive changes, use the a+b+(ab/100) shortcut to get the net percentage directly when only the final net effect is needed.
For reverse-percentage questions, divide by (1 ± %) — never multiply by the complementary percentage.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Percentage = (Part/Whole) × 100; percentage change is always relative to the OLD value, and successive changes combine multiplicatively, not by addition.
keyFacts: x% of y = y% of x.
Net of two successive % changes a and b ≈ a + b + (ab/100).
Reverse percentage: divide the final value by (1 ± %), don't subtract the percentage.
Percentage points ≠ percentage change — read which one the question means.
commonConfusion: A +10% then −10% change is a net −1%, not 0% — the second change acts on a different (already changed) base.

highYieldFacts: Successive % change formula: a + b + (ab/100), sign-aware.
Reverse percentage divides by (1 ± %); it never subtracts the percentage from the final value directly.
commonTraps: Assuming equal-magnitude rise and fall cancel to zero net change.
Percentage change computed against the new value instead of the old value.
mustRemember: x% of y always equals y% of x — swap to whichever number gives an easier fraction.

confusedTerms.distinction: 20%→25% is a 5-percentage-point rise, but a 25% relative increase in the rate — the two numbers describe the same move differently.
